feedback: If a learner adds a constant (e.g. gives ~18 km for 15 miles by adding ~1 km per mile), show that 15 miles = 3 × 5 miles, so the km must also triple (8 → 24); plot the additive point to see it leave the origin line.

If a learner divides or gives fewer km than miles (~9 km), remind them a mile is the longer unit: 5 miles needs 8 km to cover the same distance, so any distance is a bigger number of km than of miles.
Reinforce that each answer is 'about': ≈ means approximately, so 24 km is a sensible estimate (true value ~24.14 km), not exact.
activities.intendedInsight: Converting means scaling the ratio 5:8 (multiplying), which keeps every point on the same straight line through zero; adding a constant to both quantities knocks points off that line and is wrong.
learnerActions: Work with a double number line AND a matching ratio table, both with miles and km aligned from 0, showing the pairs 5↔8, 10↔16, 15↔24.

Scale the ratio up and down multiplicatively: state that 15 miles is 3 lots of 5 miles, so it is 3 lots of 8 km = 24 km; extend to 40 miles ≈ 64 km (×8), and confirm the ×1.6 'between the lines' multiplier.

Connect the pairs to a conversion graph: plot the pairs and confirm they lie on one straight line through the origin (with miles on the horizontal axis and km on the vertical axis, the gradient is about 1.6).

Then try a character's 'add 5 to both' shortcut (5 miles, 8 km → 10 miles, 13 km) and plot that point; notice it falls OFF the origin line (the true pair is 10 miles ↔ 16 km) and explain why the shortcut is wrong.
Use a compare task: place a 10 km race and a 6-mile run (≈ 9.6 km) on the same line and decide which reaches further (the 10 km race).
activities.title: Slide and scale: the conversion stays on one straight line

feedback: For the '23 km' example: adding 15 to both does not preserve the 5:8 ratio; scale instead — 20 miles is 4 lots of 5 miles, so 4 lots of 8 km = 32 km.
If ~18 km is chosen: this comes from starting at 5 mi ≈ 8 km and adding ~1 km per extra mile; triple the whole ratio instead (8 → 24 km for 15 miles).
If ~9 km is chosen: this divides and treats a km as the larger unit; a mile is longer, so the km figure must be larger than the mile figure (about 24 km).
activities.intendedInsight: Recognising and articulating the additive error consolidates that conversion scales the ratio; the characteristic wrong answers (~18 km additive, ~9 km wrong-direction) typically come from misreading the proportional structure or the direction of conversion rather than from arithmetic slips.
learnerActions: Read a character's converted answer and decide if it is right, e.g. '5 miles ≈ 8 km, so 20 miles ≈ 8 + 15 = 23 km'.
Identify the wrong strategy (adding a constant to both quantities) and compute the correct answer multiplicatively (20 miles = 4 × 5 miles = 4 × 8 km = 32 km).
Convert 15 miles and choose among sensible and faulty options, explaining why the additive (~18 km) and wrong-direction (~9 km) options are wrong.
Explain the error in words: why does adding the same amount to both quantities break the proportion?
activities.title: Spot the mistake: additive versus multiplicative conversion
